title: PadhoAI
tagline: Board exam prep for small town students
pitch: You quit your job to build an exam prep app for Hindi medium Class 10 students in small towns. You have ₹1.5 crore from angel investors and two co-founders. In about two years you must reach 50,000 monthly students, earn as much as you spend each month, and keep parents' trust.

stages.title: Find the real problem
stages.situation: You want to help Class 10 students in small towns pass their board exams. Before building, you want to know why so many struggle. You have one month.

options.label: Run an Instagram poll for students
options.outcome: 5,000 replies. Most say they want 'more videos' and 'celebrity teachers'.
options.lesson: Online polls reach the students who are already online and confident. The ones who struggle most are often not there.

later.note: Students who joined for 'more videos' watched a few and stopped. Videos were never the real problem.

options.label: Sit in 5 coaching classes and visit 20 homes in Gorakhpur and Patna
options.detail: Slow, but you see real study habits.
options.outcome: You find the real pain: students study in Hindi, but most good material is in English, and nobody answers their doubts after 8 PM.
options.lesson: Seeing real users in their real setting shows the problem behind the request. That insight shapes the whole product.

options.label: Skip research and copy the biggest ed tech app
options.outcome: You save a month, but you don't know what small town Hindi medium students need.
options.lesson: Copying a leader copies their answers without their reasons. You can't beat them at their own game.

stages.title: Pick your first users
stages.situation: You can't serve everyone at the start. Which group do you build for first?

options.label: Hindi medium Class 10 students in UP and Bihar
options.detail: One exam, one language, a clear deadline.
options.outcome: A tight group with an urgent goal. Word spreads fast between classmates.
options.lesson: A narrow first user lets you build something they truly love. You can widen later.

options.label: Every student from Class 6 to 12, all boards
options.outcome: You need content for 7 classes and many boards. The team is stretched thin.
options.lesson: Serving everyone at once makes the product average for each group. Costs grow faster than love.

options.label: JEE engineering aspirants
options.detail: They spend the most on coaching.
options.outcome: Many sign up, but they compare you with the giants every day.
options.lesson: A rich market full of strong rivals is a hard first fight. Having money to spend is not the same as needing you.

later.note: After the JEE mock results, your aspirants moved to the big coaching brands they already trusted.

stages.title: Build the first version
stages.situation: You have two months to launch something students can use.

options.label: Short Hindi lessons plus a daily 10-question quiz, for 3 subjects
options.detail: Works on cheap phones and slow internet.
options.outcome: Small and fast. Students finish a lesson on the bus and come back for the quiz.
options.lesson: An MVP should solve the core problem well for the first users. Small and loved beats big and average.

options.label: Live classes in every subject with 20 teachers
options.outcome: It looks great, but half the classes have fewer than 10 students and costs are huge.
options.lesson: Building everything before you know what users value burns cash on things nobody uses.

options.label: An AI chat bot that answers any question
options.detail: Cheap to build with a ready model.
options.outcome: Students love it at first. Then it starts giving confident wrong answers.
options.lesson: New tech is not a product. In exam prep, one wrong answer can cost a student marks, so accuracy matters more than magic.

later.note: A screenshot of your bot giving a wrong Science answer went viral in a teachers' WhatsApp group.

stages.title: Set the price
stages.situation: Students have little money. Parents decide what to pay for. How will you charge?

options.label: Free lessons, ₹149 a month for tests and doubt solving
options.outcome: Most stay free, but about 1 in 8 parents pay for tests before exams.
options.lesson: Free value brings users in. A clear paid step for the moment that matters most (exams) turns them into revenue.

options.label: Everything free for the first year
options.outcome: Users pour in. So do your video and server bills.
options.lesson: Free with no plan to charge trains users that your product is worth nothing.

later.note: You started charging to stop the losses. Many students who came for free left the same week.

options.label: ₹499 a year, sold through school teachers
options.outcome: Fewer sign ups, but students whose teacher recommends you stick around.
options.lesson: A trusted person recommending you is a strong channel, though it grows slower.

stages.title: Launch
stages.situation: Your first version is ready. How do you get the first big wave of students?

options.label: Free chapter videos on YouTube and Telegram study groups
options.outcome: Your Hindi chapter summaries get shared before the half yearly exams.
options.lesson: Starting where users already gather is cheap and builds trust.

options.label: ₹30 lakh on Instagram and YouTube ads
options.outcome: Installs jump. Many open the app once.
options.lesson: Paid users often have low intent. Measure if they stay, not just if they arrive.

later.note: Most students from ads tried one lesson and never came back.

options.label: Referral: one free month of tests for both friends
options.outcome: Whole classes join together.
options.lesson: Referrals bring users similar to your best users, and they keep bringing more.

stages.title: First week experience
stages.situation: Half of new students never finish their first lesson. What do you fix?

options.label: A 3 minute starter quiz that finds each student's weakest chapter
options.outcome: Students see 'Start here' on day one. First lesson completion doubles.
options.lesson: Activation is getting users to the first moment of value fast. A personal start makes that moment clear.

options.label: Push alerts: 'Your rank is falling!' three times a day
options.outcome: Clicks go up for a week. Parents complain the app stresses their children.
options.lesson: Notifications that scare people may lift clicks but hurt trust, especially with young users.

options.label: Give coins for every daily login
options.outcome: Logins rise. Many open the app, collect coins and leave.
options.lesson: Rewarding the wrong action builds the wrong habit. Reward learning, not opening.

stages.title: Choose your north star
stages.situation: Your investors want one number the whole team works on each week.

options.label: Students who finish at least 3 lessons and quizzes a week
options.outcome: The team improves lessons, quiz quality and doubt answers. Students get better marks.
options.lesson: A good north star measures the value users get. Grow that and revenue follows.

options.label: App installs
options.outcome: Marketing wins, product suffers. Installs go up, learning doesn't.
options.lesson: Vanity metrics feel good but don't show if users get value.

options.label: Minutes of video watched
options.outcome: The team makes videos longer. Students watch more but learn less, and video costs rise.
options.lesson: A metric can be gamed. More time is not always more value.

stages.title: Grow the team
stages.situation: You have 12,000 students and the founders are worn out. Who do you hire?

options.label: 2 senior teachers who also think like product people
options.detail: They shape lessons and quiz quality.
options.outcome: Lesson quality jumps. The founders finally sleep.
options.lesson: Early hires should be strong in the area that matters most to users.

options.label: 15 tele callers to sell to parents
options.outcome: Sales go up. So do complaints about calls at dinner time.
options.lesson: Pushy sales can grow revenue on paper while it quietly destroys trust.

later.note: Parents posted recordings of your callers promising 'guaranteed 90%'. Refund requests are piling up.

options.label: Stay lean, founders record every lesson
options.outcome: You save money but the team is exhausted.
options.lesson: Burnout is a real cost, even when it isn't on the spreadsheet.

later.note: Tired founders shipped a lesson with wrong formulas just before exams.

stages.title: Raise money
stages.situation: Investors are interested. How much do you raise?

options.label: ₹10 crore, promise 8 states and 5 languages in a year
options.outcome: Huge cash. Huge expectations.
options.lesson: A big round comes with promises. Grow before your product is ready and costs explode.

later.note: To keep your promise, you launched in Marathi, Bengali and Tamil before Hindi was profitable. Costs exploded.

options.label: ₹3 crore from founders of ed tech and coaching businesses
options.outcome: Enough runway, and investors who know how exam prep works.
options.lesson: Smart money brings advice and contacts, not just cash.

options.label: Don't raise. Aim for profit.
options.outcome: You stay careful, but growth slows.
options.lesson: Not raising is a valid choice, but you need a clear path to profit soon.

stages.title: Build a growth engine
stages.situation: You want growth that keeps going on its own. What do you build?

options.label: Add Class 12 and 4 more subjects
options.outcome: Users grow, but so do content costs.
options.lesson: Expanding the catalogue helps growth, but each new subject costs money until it pays for itself.

options.label: TV ads on Hindi news channels
options.outcome: A big spike in sign ups. Many are parents who don't know what the app does.
options.lesson: Expensive spikes don't build lasting growth.

later.note: Most people who installed after the TV ad never opened a lesson.

options.label: Weekly class challenge: friends take the same test and share score cards
options.detail: A loop students run for you.
options.outcome: Score cards spread across school WhatsApp groups every Sunday.
options.lesson: A growth loop turns users' own activity into new users. Duolingo leagues and Wordle grids work this way.

stages.title: Earn more per student
stages.situation: You need more money per student. What do you try?

options.label: Sell ads to local coaching centres
options.outcome: Some money comes in. Some parents find the ads confusing.
options.lesson: Ads can work, but they must not hurt the core experience.

options.label: Raise the price to ₹299 a month
options.outcome: Revenue jumps, but families in small towns feel priced out.
options.lesson: Price rises need to match the value users see.

options.label: Printed revision books and sample papers, ordered in the app
options.outcome: Slow start. Then sales pick up before exams.
options.lesson: Selling something users already buy, in a better way, builds margin over time.

later.note: Your revision books became a best seller before boards. Margins on them are double.

stages.title: A giant enters
stages.situation: A famous ed tech company launches a free Hindi Class 10 batch with a celebrity teacher.

options.label: Make everything free to match them
options.outcome: Users stay, but you are burning cash fast.
options.lesson: Price wars favour the player with the most money. That's rarely you.

later.note: The giant's free batch ended. Your cash is gone, and deal seekers left for the next free offer.

options.label: Ignore price. Double down on fast doubt answers in Hindi
options.outcome: Some students try the free batch. Many find it too crowded to ask doubts.
options.lesson: Compete on your strengths, not on what rivals choose.

later.note: Students came back, saying the free batch never answered their questions.

options.label: Pivot to selling to schools instead
options.outcome: School sales are slow and the team is confused.
options.lesson: Pivots can save a company, but running from competition loses what you built.

stages.title: A crisis
stages.situation: One of your teachers posted 'these questions WILL come in boards'. They didn't. Angry parents are trending.

options.label: Apologise, refund that month to everyone, publish a content check rule
options.outcome: It costs money, but parents respect the honesty.
options.lesson: Handling a crisis openly can build more trust than you had before.

options.label: Send legal notices to the parents posting about it
options.outcome: This becomes the bigger story.
options.lesson: Fighting customers in public makes a crisis much worse.

options.label: Blame the teacher in a public post
options.outcome: Users see it as dodging. Your other teachers are upset.
options.lesson: Users hold you responsible for your whole product, including the people you hire.

stages.title: Teachers want a better deal
stages.situation: Your freelance teachers say pay per video is too low. Some are talking to rivals.

options.label: Raise pay and show each teacher's name and rating
options.outcome: Costs rise, but lessons get better and teachers promote you to their own followers.
options.lesson: In a marketplace, both sides need a good deal.

options.label: Replace them with AI generated videos
options.outcome: Lessons feel robotic. Students notice.
options.lesson: Cutting the people users love to save money often costs more.

options.label: Give teachers a share of test revenue from their students
options.outcome: Top teachers earn more. Some new ones struggle at first.
options.lesson: Aligning partner pay with outcomes can work, if it's fair.

stages.title: The road to profit
stages.situation: Investors want a clear path to profit before the next round.

options.label: Stop the 3 least used subjects and the live studio
options.outcome: Some students leave, but costs fall a lot.
options.lesson: Cutting losing parts focuses the business on what works.

options.label: Launch in Tamil and Bengali now
options.outcome: Big new costs before the core is profitable.
options.lesson: Expanding to escape problems usually multiplies them.

options.label: Raise prices 5% on everything
options.outcome: Revenue goes up a bit. Some families leave.
options.lesson: Small price changes add up, but watch trust and growth.

events.title: Board results day
events.situation: Results are out. Students who used you scored well, and local news wants a story.

options.label: Share real student stories, with their permission
options.outcome: Parents trust real stories from their own towns.
options.lesson: Proof from real users is the strongest marketing.

options.label: Run ads saying '100% students passed'
options.outcome: A journalist checks and finds it isn't true.
options.lesson: Claims you can't prove damage trust fast.

events.title: Servers crash in exam week
events.situation: The night before the Science exam, your app goes down for 3 hours.

options.label: Post free PDFs on Telegram right away and say sorry
options.outcome: Students still get the notes and thank you.
options.lesson: In a crisis, give users another way to get what they need.

options.label: Stay quiet and fix it
options.outcome: Students panic and ask in every group what's going on.
options.lesson: Silence in a crisis feels like not caring.

events.title: A rival poaches your best teacher
events.situation: Your most popular Maths teacher has an offer at double the pay.

options.label: Counter-offer with equity
options.outcome: They stay, and other teachers see you value them.
options.lesson: Key people are worth investing in.

options.label: Let them go and promote a new teacher
options.outcome: Some students follow the old teacher.
options.lesson: Losing key people has a cost. Plan for it.

events.title: New rules for ed tech sales
events.situation: The government publishes new rules: no pressure selling to parents and easy refunds.

options.label: Follow them right away and say so publicly
options.outcome: Some sales drop, but parents feel safe.
options.lesson: Following rules early builds trust and avoids bigger trouble.

options.label: Wait and see if anyone enforces them
options.outcome: A complaint becomes a fine and a news story.
options.lesson: Rules for user safety are a floor, not an option.
